git-blob-id.title: Compute a blob's object id
git-blob-id.description:
Git names every stored file by a hash of its content. For a file whose content is the byte string
`data`, the object id is the SHA-1 digest (40 lowercase hex characters) of

```
b"blob " + <decimal length of data in BYTES> + b"\0" + data
```

Write `blob_id(content)` that takes the file content as a Python `str`, encodes it as UTF-8 and returns
the object id. The length in the header counts **bytes after encoding**, not characters.

**Example:** `blob_id("")` → `"e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391"` (the famous empty blob)

**Example:** `blob_id("hello\n")` → `"ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a"`

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Objects: blobs, trees, commits and tags*. Python `bytes` versus `str`, and `hashlib`.
guide.intuition: Git does not hash the raw file. It first glues a tiny header in front that says what kind of object this is and how long it is, then hashes header and content together. Reproduce that byte sequence exactly and the standard SHA-1 function gives you the same id that `git hash-object` prints.
hints: Hash functions work on bytes. Convert the string with `.encode('utf-8')` before doing anything else.
The header is the word `blob`, one space, the length written in decimal digits, and a single zero byte.
Take `len()` of the encoded bytes, not of the original string: `'é'` is one character but two bytes.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing to search here, so the 'naive' version is the common wrong one: hashing only the content. It gives a valid SHA-1, just not the one Git uses, so no object would ever be found under it.
guide.approach:
1. `data = content.encode('utf-8')`.
2. Build `header = b'blob ' + str(len(data)).encode() + b'\0'`.
3. Return `hashlib.sha1(header + data).hexdigest()`.

**Dry run** for `'hello\n'`: the data is 6 bytes, so the header is `blob 6\0` (7 bytes). The 13 bytes `blob 6\0hello\n` hash to `ce0136...`, which is what `echo hello | git hash-object --stdin` prints.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the content size because SHA-1 reads each byte once; space O(n) for the encoded copy.
guide.pitfalls: Using the character count instead of the byte count (breaks on any non-ASCII text). Writing the NUL as the two characters backslash-zero inside a raw string. Adding a newline the caller did not supply: `'hello'` and `'hello\n'` are different blobs.
guide.follow_up: Trees and commits use the same scheme with the words `tree` and `commit` in the header; the next problem builds on that.

git-tree-commit-id.title: Hash a tree and a commit (simplified format)
git-tree-commit-id.description:
Real Git stores trees in a binary layout. This problem uses a **text-only simplified layout** so you can
focus on the idea: a commit names a tree, a tree names blobs, and every id is a hash of content.

Every object id is `sha1(f"{kind} {len(body)}\0".encode() + body)` as 40 hex characters, where `body`
is UTF-8 bytes and `len` is its length in bytes.

**Tree body.** You get `entries`, a list of `[mode, name, object_id]`. Sort the entries by `name`
(plain string order) and write one line per entry:

```
<mode> <name>\t<object_id>\n
```

The kind is `tree`. An empty entry list gives an empty body.

**Commit body.** Kind `commit`, built from these lines in this order:

```
tree <tree_id>\n
parent <parent_id>\n        (one line per parent, in the order given; none for a root commit)
author <author>\n
\n
<message>\n
```

Write `commit_id(entries, parents, author, message)` returning `[tree_id, commit_id]`.

**Example:** `commit_id([], [], "Ada", "init")` → the tree id is `sha1(b"tree 0\0")`, which is
`4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904` (the real empty-tree id, since an empty body is the same in both layouts).

guide.prereqs: Problem *Compute a blob's object id* and the internals lesson on the four object types.
guide.intuition: A commit id is a hash of text that contains the tree id, and the tree id is a hash of text that contains blob ids. Change one byte in one file and the blob id changes, so the tree body changes, so the tree id changes, so the commit body changes. That chain is why a commit id pins down the entire snapshot and all history behind it.
hints: Write one helper that takes a kind and a body string and returns the id. You will call it twice.
Entries must be sorted so that the same set of files always produces the same tree id, no matter the input order.
Parents are NOT sorted: the first parent is special in Git, so their order is part of the commit's identity.
guide.brute_force: No search is involved. The straightforward construction is already optimal; the only way to go wrong is to assemble the bytes in a different shape from the specification.
guide.approach:
1. Sort entries by name and join `mode name<TAB>id<NEWLINE>` lines into the tree body.
2. Hash it with kind `tree`.
3. Build the commit body: `tree` line, one `parent` line each, `author` line, blank line, message, newline.
4. Hash it with kind `commit` and return both ids.

**Dry run** for no entries, no parents, author `Ada`, message `init`: tree body is empty, so the tree id is `sha1('tree 0\0')` = `4b825d...`. The commit body is `tree 4b825d...\nauthor Ada\n\ninit\n`, 63 bytes, hashed behind the header `commit 63\0`.
guide.complexity: Time O(e log e + n) for e entries and n total bytes; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting to sort entries, or sorting parents. Counting characters instead of bytes in the header (the non-ASCII test catches it). Dropping the blank line between the headers and the message.
guide.follow_up: Real trees store the id as 20 raw bytes and sort directories as if their name ended in a slash. Try `git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}` to see a real one decoded.

git-abbreviate-ids.title: Shortest unique object-id prefixes
git-abbreviate-ids.description:
`git log --oneline` shows short ids such as `3f9c2ab`. Git picks a prefix long enough to be unambiguous
among all objects in the repository, with a minimum length.

Write `abbreviate(ids, min_len)`. `ids` is a list of **distinct** lowercase hex strings, all of the same
length `L` (`min_len <= L`). For each id return the shortest prefix of length at least `min_len` that is
not a prefix of any other id in the list. Return the prefixes in the same order as the input.

**Example:** `abbreviate(["abcd12", "abcd34", "ffff00"], 4)` → `["abcd1", "abcd3", "ffff"]`

**Example:** `abbreviate(["a1b2c3"], 4)` → `["a1b2"]`

The list may hold tens of thousands of ids, so comparing every pair is too slow.

guide.prereqs: String prefixes and sorting. The lesson on revision selection explains why short ids work at all.
guide.intuition: After sorting, the ids that share the longest prefix with a given id are its immediate neighbours in the sorted list. So each id only needs to be compared with the one before and the one after it, never with the whole list.
hints: A prefix is unique when it is one character longer than the longest prefix shared with any other id.
Sort the ids. Why can the worst clash for an id only come from a sorted neighbour?
Compute the common-prefix length for each adjacent pair once and update the requirement of both members of the pair.
guide.brute_force: For each id, grow the prefix from `min_len` and scan all other ids with `startswith`. That is O(n^2 L) and takes far too long for many thousands of ids.
guide.approach:
1. Sort indices by id.
2. For each adjacent pair compute `c = common_prefix_length + 1`.
3. Each id needs `max(min_len, c_left, c_right)` characters.
4. Slice and return in input order.

**Dry run** on `abcd12, abcd34, ffff00` with minimum 4: sorted order is the same. Pair one shares `abcd` (4) so both need 5. Pair two shares nothing so needs 1, below the minimum. Result: `abcd1`, `abcd3`, `ffff`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n * L) for the sort plus O(nL) for neighbour comparisons; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Returning results in sorted order instead of input order. Forgetting the minimum length. Using only the left neighbour.
guide.follow_up: Git uses the same neighbour idea inside its sorted pack index. A trie gives the answer too, at a higher memory cost.

git-gitignore-match.title: Match .gitignore patterns
git-gitignore-match.description:
Implement a simplified `.gitignore` matcher: `is_ignored(patterns, path)` returns `True` when the **file**
at `path` (relative to the repository root, components separated by `/`, never ending in `/`) is ignored.

Process `patterns` top to bottom; the **last pattern that matches decides**. If none matches, the file is not ignored.

Rules for one pattern line:

1. Strip surrounding whitespace. Skip empty lines and lines starting with `#`.
2. A leading `!` negates the pattern: when it matches, the file becomes *not ignored*.
3. A trailing `/` means the pattern matches **directories only**. Remove it before matching.
4. If the remaining pattern contains a `/` (at the start or in the middle) it is **anchored**: it must
   match starting at the repository root. A leading `/` is then removed. A pattern with no `/` may match
   starting at **any depth**.
5. Split the pattern on `/` into segments. A segment that is exactly `**` matches zero or more whole
   path components. In any other segment `*` matches any run of characters except `/`, `?` matches
   exactly one character except `/`, and every other character (including `[` and `.`) matches itself.
6. A pattern matches the path when its segments match **the whole path**, or match **any leading
   directory of it** (for `a/b/c.txt` the leading directories are `a` and `a/b`); a matched directory
   takes everything inside with it. A directory-only pattern can only match a leading directory.

Simplification: unlike real Git, a `!` rule here *can* re-include a file inside an ignored directory.

**Example:** `is_ignored(["*.log", "!keep.log"], "logs/keep.log")` → `False`

**Example:** `is_ignored(["build/"], "app/build/out.o")` → `True`

guide.prereqs: The lesson on recording changes (the ignore-file section). Recursion over lists, and either regular expressions or a hand-written wildcard matcher.
guide.intuition: Three independent ideas are stacked: (1) the last matching line wins, which is a simple loop with a variable; (2) ignoring a directory ignores everything under it, so you test every leading directory as well as the full path; (3) anchoring, which you can remove from the picture by turning an unanchored pattern into an anchored one that starts with `**`.
hints: Deal with the decorations first: comment, `!`, trailing `/`, leading `/`. What is left is a plain list of segments.
An unanchored pattern `x` behaves exactly like the anchored pattern `**/x`. Rewrite it and you only need one matcher.
Match segment lists recursively: a `**` segment tries to swallow 0, 1, 2, ... components; any other segment must match exactly one component.
guide.brute_force: Translate the whole pattern into one giant regular expression. It works for simple cases but the interactions of anchoring, directory-only patterns and `**` make the single regex hard to get right; many attempts wrongly let `*` cross a `/`.
guide.approach:
For each pattern: strip, skip comments, record negation and directory-only flags, decide anchoring, split on `/`, and prepend `**` if unanchored. Then for `k = 1..len(parts)` test whether the segments match the first `k` components (skipping the full path when the pattern is directory-only). On a hit set `ignored = not negated`.

**Dry run** `['build/']` against `app/build/out.o`: flags `dir_only=True`, unanchored, segments `['**','build']`. Prefix `app`: `**` takes zero then `build` vs `app` fails; `**` takes one and nothing is left, fails. Prefix `app/build`: `**` takes `app`, `build` matches `build`, hit. Result `True`.
guide.complexity: With p pattern segments and d path components, the recursive match is O(p * d) per prefix in practice (exponential only with many `**`), so about O(lines * p * d^2). Paths are short, so this is fast.
guide.pitfalls: Letting `*` match across `/`. Treating `.` as a regex wildcard (the `a.b` test). Forgetting that a directory-only pattern must not match the file itself (`build/` versus a file named `build`). Returning on the first match instead of the last.
guide.follow_up: Real Git adds bracket classes like `[co]`, escaping with backslash, per-directory ignore files, and the rule that a file cannot be re-included when its parent directory is excluded. `git check-ignore -v path` tells you which line decided.

git-conventional-commit.title: Parse and validate a Conventional Commit message
git-conventional-commit.description:
Many teams require commit messages in the *Conventional Commits* shape so that changelogs and version
bumps can be automated. Write `parse_commit(message)` that validates a message and returns a dict, or
`None` if the message is invalid.

The **header** is the first line and must look like

```
<type>[(<scope>)][!]: <description>
```

- `type` is one of `feat fix docs style refactor perf test build ci chore revert` (lowercase).
- `scope` is optional; when present it is inside parentheses and consists of one or more of `a-z`, `0-9`, `-`.
- `!` is optional and marks a breaking change.
- Then exactly a colon and **one space**.
- `description` is non-empty, does not start with a space and does not end with a period.
- The whole header is at most 72 characters long.

If the message has more than one line, the **second line must be empty** (it separates header and body).

The commit is **breaking** when the header has `!`, or when any line after the header starts with
`BREAKING CHANGE: ` or `BREAKING-CHANGE: `.

Return `{"type": ..., "scope": ... or None, "description": ..., "breaking": True/False}`.

**Example:** `parse_commit("feat(api)!: drop v1 endpoints")` →
`{"type": "feat", "scope": "api", "description": "drop v1 endpoints", "breaking": True}`

**Example:** `parse_commit("Fixed stuff")` → `None`

guide.prereqs: The lesson on commit-message conventions in *Team workflows in practice*. Regular expressions with optional groups.
guide.intuition: The header is a tiny formal language, which makes it a perfect fit for one anchored regular expression with optional groups. Everything the regex cannot express conveniently (length limit, trailing period, the blank second line, footers) is a handful of plain `if` statements around it.
hints: Split the message into lines first; almost every rule talks about a specific line.
Use `re.fullmatch` so that leftovers at either end make the header invalid. Give the scope and the `!` their own optional groups.
Breaking can come from two places. Compute it from the header, then scan the remaining lines for a footer that *starts* with the marker.
guide.brute_force: Chop the header up with `split(':')`, `find('(')` and friends. It can be made to work, but every optional part doubles the cases, and loose versions accept garbage such as unknown types or uppercase scopes.
guide.approach:
1. `lines = message.split('\n')`; reject a header longer than 72.
2. Full-match `type (scope)? !? ': ' description`.
3. Reject descriptions starting with a space or ending with `.`.
4. If there is a second line it must be empty.
5. `breaking = bang or any footer line starts with the marker`.

**Dry run** `feat(api)!: drop v1 endpoints`: groups are `feat`, `api`, `!`, `drop v1 endpoints`; one line only, so no body checks; breaking is true from the bang.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n) in the message length.
guide.pitfalls: Using `match` instead of `fullmatch`. Accepting `chore:no space`. Counting the 72 limit on the description instead of the whole header. Detecting the breaking marker in the middle of a sentence.
guide.follow_up: Map the result to a semantic-version bump: breaking → major, `feat` → minor, `fix` → patch. Tools such as commitlint apply rules like these in a `commit-msg` hook.

git-sort-version-tags.title: Sort version tags
git-sort-version-tags.description:
`git tag` lists tags alphabetically, which puts `v1.10.0` before `v1.9.0`. Write `sort_tags(tags)` that
returns the valid version tags in ascending **semantic version** order and silently drops everything else.

A valid tag is: an optional leading `v`, then `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` (three non-negative decimal integers),
then optionally `-` followed by a pre-release made of one or more dot-separated identifiers, each
consisting of one or more of `0-9 A-Z a-z -`.

Ordering:

1. Compare major, minor, patch numerically.
2. A version **with** a pre-release is lower than the same version without one (`1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0`).
3. Two pre-releases are compared identifier by identifier: identifiers made only of digits compare
   numerically; a numeric identifier is lower than a non-numeric one; two non-numeric identifiers compare
   as plain strings; if all shared identifiers are equal, the one with fewer identifiers is lower.
4. Tags that compare equal (for example `v1.0.0` and `1.0.0`) keep their input order.

**Example:** `sort_tags(["v1.10.0", "v1.9.0", "v1.9.0-rc.1", "latest"])` → `["v1.9.0-rc.1", "v1.9.0", "v1.10.0"]`

guide.prereqs: The tagging lesson. Python tuple comparison and `sort` with a `key` (and the fact that Python's sort is stable).
guide.intuition: Sorting is easy once every tag is turned into a key whose natural tuple ordering equals the ordering you want. The art is in designing the key: numbers as ints, a flag that pushes releases after pre-releases, and a per-identifier triple that makes numeric identifiers sort before textual ones.
hints: Validate with one regular expression and capture the three numbers and the optional pre-release.
Give a release the key `(1, ())` and a pre-release `(0, identifiers)`. Tuples compare element by element, so the flag settles rule 2.
Encode a numeric identifier as `(0, number, '')` and a textual one as `(1, 0, text)`. Tuple comparison then implements rule 3, including the shorter-is-lower case.
guide.brute_force: Write a `cmp(a, b)` function with nested ifs and use `functools.cmp_to_key`. It is correct if careful, but long and easy to get subtly wrong; plain string sorting, the really naive approach, fails as soon as a number reaches two digits.
guide.approach:
Parse, build `(core, pre_key)` for each valid tag, sort by key (stable, so equal versions keep input order), and return the tags.

**Dry run** on `v1.10.0, v1.9.0, v1.9.0-rc.1, latest`: `latest` fails the regex. Keys: `((1,10,0),(1,()))`, `((1,9,0),(1,()))`, `((1,9,0),(0,((1,0,'rc'),(0,1,''))))`. Sorting puts the rc first (flag 0), then 1.9.0, then 1.10.0.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) comparisons on short keys; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing numbers as strings. Treating the pre-release as one string so that `rc.10 < rc.9`. Mixing ints and strings in one tuple position, which raises `TypeError` in Python 3. Accepting a capital `V` or an empty identifier.
guide.follow_up: Git can do this itself: `git tag --sort=version:refname` (alias `-v:refname`), with `versionsort.suffix` controlling pre-release suffixes.

git-parse-refspec.title: Parse a refspec
git-parse-refspec.description:
A refspec tells `git fetch` and `git push` which references to transfer and where to put them, for
example `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`.

Write `parse_refspec(spec)` returning a dict
`{"force": bool, "src": str, "dst": str or None, "pattern": bool}` or `None` if the spec is invalid
under these simplified rules:

1. An optional leading `+` sets `force` and is removed.
2. If there is no `:`, the whole rest is `src` and `dst` is `None`. With exactly one `:`, the left side is
   `src` and the right side is `dst`. More than one `:` is invalid.
3. Whitespace anywhere is invalid. `src` and `dst` may not both be missing/empty.
4. An empty `dst` after a colon (`main:`) is invalid. An empty `src` before a colon (`:topic`) is valid and
   means "delete `dst`"; it cannot be combined with a `*`.
5. Each side may contain at most one `*`. When `dst` is present, either both sides contain a `*` or
   neither does. Without a `dst`, `src` may not contain a `*`.
6. `pattern` is `True` when the refspec uses `*`.

**Example:** `parse_refspec("+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*")` →
`{"force": True, "src": "refs/heads/*", "dst": "refs/remotes/origin/*", "pattern": True}`

**Example:** `parse_refspec("main")` → `{"force": False, "src": "main", "dst": None, "pattern": False}`

guide.prereqs: The internals lesson on the refspec. Basic string methods.
guide.intuition: A refspec is `[+]source[:destination]`. Peel the pieces off from the outside in (plus sign, then the colon split), then run the consistency checks on the two halves. No clever algorithm is needed; the exercise is about being exhaustive with the rules.
hints: Handle the `+` first and remember it in a boolean; the rest of the logic should never see it.
`str.count(':')` tells you which of the three shapes you have: no colon, one colon, or invalid.
The wildcard rule is an equality of two booleans: `('*' in src) == ('*' in dst)`.
guide.brute_force: A single regular expression can validate most of this, but the 'star on both sides or neither' rule needs a lookahead or a second check anyway, and the result is harder to read than straight-line code.
guide.approach:
Reject whitespace; strip `+`; count colons; split; reject empty destination or totally empty spec; check star counts; compute `pattern`.

**Dry run** `:topic`: no plus, one colon, `src=''`, `dst='topic'`, no stars on either side, so the result is a delete refspec with `pattern` false. **Dry run** `refs/heads/*`: no colon so `dst=None`, but `src` has a star, invalid.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n) in the length of the string.
guide.pitfalls: `lstrip('+')` removes several plus signs. `split(':', 1)` hides the three-part error. Forgetting that `:dst` is legal while `src:` is not (in this problem's rules).
guide.follow_up: Write `map_ref(spec, name)` that returns the destination name for a concrete source ref by substituting what the `*` matched; that is exactly what fetch does to build remote-tracking names.

git-is-ancestor.title: Can this branch fast-forward?
git-is-ancestor.description:
A history is given as a dict `parents` mapping every commit id to the list of its parent ids (empty
list for a root commit). A branch pointing at `current` can be **fast-forwarded** to `target` exactly
when `current` is an ancestor of `target`: you can reach `current` from `target` by following parent
links zero or more times. (Zero links means a commit counts as its own ancestor.)

Write `can_fast_forward(parents, current, target)` returning `True` or `False`.

Histories may be thousands of commits deep, so a recursive walk will overflow the stack.

**Example:** with `A <- B <- C` (`{"A": [], "B": ["A"], "C": ["B"]}`), `can_fast_forward(p, "A", "C")` → `True`
and `can_fast_forward(p, "C", "A")` → `False`.

guide.prereqs: The branching lessons (fast-forward merges). Depth-first or breadth-first search with a visited set.
guide.intuition: Commits only know their parents, so the natural direction to walk is backwards in time. Start at the newer commit (`target`) and explore everything reachable; if you bump into `current`, then `target` already contains all of `current`'s history and the branch label can simply slide forward.
hints: Which commit should the search start from? Parent links point from new to old.
A merge commit has several parents. Following only the first one misses whole side branches.
Use an explicit stack and a `seen` set; without the set, histories with many merges are revisited exponentially often.
guide.brute_force: Recursive DFS without a visited set: correct on tiny inputs, but it re-explores shared history once per path (exponential with repeated merges) and dies with `RecursionError` on a long chain.
guide.approach:
Iterative DFS from `target`. Pop a commit; if it equals `current` return `True`; otherwise push its unseen parents. If the stack empties, return `False`.

**Dry run** on the sample graph asking `D -> M`: stack `[M]`; pop M, push E and F; pop F, push D; pop D, equals current, return `True`. Asking `C -> F`: from F we see D, B, A and never C, so `False`: `main` at C and `feature` at F have diverged.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) in the part of the graph reachable from `target`; space O(V) for the visited set.
guide.pitfalls: Searching from `current` (you cannot walk towards children). Following only first parents. Forgetting the reflexive case `current == target`.
guide.follow_up: `git merge-base --is-ancestor A B` answers exactly this with its exit status. Git speeds it up using commit dates/generation numbers to stop early.

git-merge-base.title: Find the merge base
git-merge-base.description:
The **merge base** of two commits is their best common ancestor: the point where the two lines of
history last agreed. A three-way merge compares both tips against it.

`parents` maps every commit id to its list of parent ids. A commit counts as its own ancestor.
A *common ancestor* of `a` and `b` is a commit that is an ancestor of both. A common ancestor is **best**
if it is not a (proper) ancestor of any other common ancestor.

Write `merge_base(parents, a, b)` returning the **sorted list** of all best common ancestors. Usually it
has one element; with unrelated histories it is empty; after a criss-cross merge it can have several.

**Example:** `main` is `A <- B <- C`, and `feature` forked at B: `A <- B <- D`.
`merge_base(p, "C", "D")` → `["B"]`

**Example:** `merge_base(p, "B", "D")` → `["B"]` (B is an ancestor of D, so the base is B itself)

guide.prereqs: Problem *Can this branch fast-forward?* and the lesson on basic merging. Set operations.
guide.intuition: Collect everything reachable from `a`, everything reachable from `b`, and intersect: those are the common ancestors. Most of them are uninteresting old history. The best ones are the 'newest layer' of that intersection, the common ancestors that no other common ancestor sits on top of.
hints: Reuse the reachability walk from the previous problem, but collect the whole visited set instead of stopping early.
The set of common ancestors is closed: every parent of a common ancestor is itself a common ancestor.
Because of that closure, a common ancestor is dominated exactly when it is the *parent* of some other common ancestor. Subtract all such parents.
guide.brute_force: For every pair of common ancestors (x, y) run a reachability test to see whether x is an ancestor of y, and drop x if so. That is O(k^2) walks for k common ancestors, far too slow on a long shared history.
guide.approach:
1. `A = ancestors(a)`, `B = ancestors(b)`, `common = A & B`.
2. `dominated = union of parents[c] for c in common`.
3. Return `sorted(common - dominated)`.

**Dry run** on the sample graph for `E` and `F`: ancestors(E) = {E, C, B, A}; ancestors(F) = {F, D, B, A}; common = {B, A}. Parents of B are {A}; parents of A are {}. dominated = {A}. Answer `['B']`. For the criss-cross graph and tips X, Y: common = {P, Q, R}, dominated = {R}, answer `['P', 'Q']`, which is why Git's default merge strategy first merges P and Q into a virtual base.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) for the two walks and one pass over the common set; space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Returning all common ancestors. Walking only first parents (misses bases reached through a merge). Returning the *oldest* common ancestor (the root) instead of the newest.
guide.follow_up: `git merge-base A B` prints one best base, `--all` prints every one. For more than two commits `git merge-base --octopus` intersects them all.

git-rev-range.title: Commits in the range A..B
git-rev-range.description:
The double-dot range `A..B` selects every commit that is **reachable from B but not reachable from A**
(a commit is reachable from itself). It answers "what does B have that A does not?", for example
`origin/main..HEAD` lists what you are about to push.

`parents` maps each commit id to its list of parent ids. Write `rev_range(parents, a, b)` returning the
selected commit ids as a **sorted list**.

**Example:** `main` is `A <- B <- C` and `topic` forked from B with commits `D <- E`.
`rev_range(p, "C", "E")` → `["D", "E"]` and `rev_range(p, "E", "C")` → `["C"]`.

guide.prereqs: Reachability on the commit graph (previous problems) and the lesson on revision selection.
guide.intuition: Think of each commit as standing for the *set* of commits in its history. `A..B` is then nothing more than set subtraction: history of B minus history of A.
hints: Write a function that returns the set of all commits reachable from one commit.
Call it twice. Which set do you subtract from which?
The range is not symmetric and not 'the commits between A and B on a line': with a merge inside, it includes both sides of the merge.
guide.brute_force: Walk from B and, for each commit met, run a fresh ancestor test against A. That costs a full traversal per commit, O(V * (V + E)).
guide.approach:
`sorted(ancestors(b) - ancestors(a))`.

**Dry run** on the sample graph for `E..M`: ancestors(M) = {M, E, F, C, D, B, A}; ancestors(E) = {E, C, B, A}; difference = {M, F, D}: the merge commit plus the two feature commits it brought in.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E); space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Subtracting in the wrong direction. Walking a single parent chain from B until A is found: A might not be on that chain at all, and merges add commits off the chain.
guide.follow_up: `A...B` (three dots) is the symmetric difference: commits reachable from exactly one side. `^A B` is another spelling of `A..B`, and you can exclude several tips at once.

git-log-order.title: git log order: topological with newest-first ties
git-log-order.description:
`git log --date-order` lists commits so that **no parent is shown before any of its children**, and
among the commits that are currently allowed to be shown it prefers the **newest** one.

`commits` maps each id to `{"date": int, "parents": [ids]}`. Starting from `start`, consider only commits
reachable from it. Produce the order by repeating:

- A commit is *ready* when every reachable commit that lists it as a parent has already been output
  (`start` is ready at the beginning).
- Output the ready commit with the **largest date**; break ties by the **smallest id** (string order).

Return the list of ids. Dates are not trustworthy: a child may carry an older date than its parent
(a wrong clock), and the parent must still come after the child.

**Example:** `A(10) <- B(20) <- C(30)`, `log_order(c, "C")` → `["C", "B", "A"]`

guide.prereqs: The history-viewing lesson. Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting and Python's `heapq`.
guide.intuition: This is Kahn's topological sort run 'backwards' (children before parents), with the usual queue swapped for a priority queue so that, whenever several commits are allowed next, the newest wins. The topological constraint guarantees sane output even when timestamps lie.
hints: First find the set of commits reachable from `start`; children outside that set must not count.
For every reachable commit count how many reachable children it has. A commit becomes ready when that counter hits zero.
Keep ready commits in a heap keyed by `(-date, id)` so the pop order is newest first, then smallest id.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly scan all remaining commits to find the ready ones and pick the best: O(V^2) or worse. Simply sorting by date is not a solution at all, because it breaks the parent-after-child rule under clock skew.
guide.approach:
1. DFS from `start` to get the reachable set.
2. `pending[p]` = number of reachable children of p.
3. Push `start`. Pop the best ready commit, append it, decrement `pending` for each parent, push parents that reach zero.

**Dry run** on the skewed history (A100, B90 child of A, C95 child of B, D300 child of A, M200 merging C and D), start M: output M; C and D become ready; D(300) is newer so D; A still waits for B. Then C, then B, then A. Result `M D C B A`. Plain date sorting would have printed D first and A before C.
guide.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V) because each commit enters the heap once; space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Counting children that are not reachable from `start`. Pushing a parent as soon as it is first seen rather than when its last child is output (the second wrong solution; that is how plain `git log` without ordering flags behaves, and it can show a parent before a child). Using a min-heap on date without negating.
guide.follow_up: `--topo-order` additionally avoids interleaving two lines of development; `--author-date-order` uses the author timestamp. `--graph` implies topological ordering.

git-resolve-revision.title: Resolve revision expressions like HEAD~2^2
git-resolve-revision.description:
Git lets you name commits relative to others. Implement the two most common suffixes.

- `parents` maps every commit id to its **ordered** list of parent ids (first parent first).
- `refs` maps names such as `"HEAD"`, `"main"`, `"v1.0"` to commit ids.
- `expr` is a base name followed by zero or more suffixes:
  - `~n` : follow the **first parent** `n` times. `~` alone means `~1`; `~0` is the commit itself.
  - `^n` : take the **n-th parent** (1-based) of the current commit. `^` alone means `^1`; `^0` is the commit itself.

The base name is looked up in `refs` first; if it is not a ref it must be a commit id present in `parents`.
Suffixes apply left to right. Return the resulting commit id, or `None` if the base name is unknown, the
expression is malformed, or a requested parent does not exist.

**Example:** in the history below, with `refs = {"HEAD": "M"}` and `M`'s parents `["E", "F"]`:
`resolve(p, refs, "HEAD^2")` → `"F"`, `resolve(p, refs, "HEAD~2")` → `"C"`, `resolve(p, refs, "HEAD^2~1")` → `"D"`.

```
A - B - C - E - M
     \         /
      D ----- F
```

guide.prereqs: The lesson on revision selection (ancestry references).
guide.intuition: Both suffixes are tiny instructions for a cursor sitting on a commit. `~n` means 'step to the first parent, n times' (go back n generations along the main line). `^n` means 'step once, to parent number n' (choose which side of a merge). Parse the string into a list of such instructions and execute them in order.
hints: Split the expression into a base name and a suffix string; a regular expression such as `[~^]\d*` then tokenises the suffixes.
`~3` is three steps; `^3` is one step to the third parent. They only coincide for n = 1.
Check for a missing parent at every single step and return `None` immediately.
guide.brute_force: Character-by-character scanning with manual index bookkeeping works but is error-prone around multi-digit numbers and the implicit 1. There is no asymptotically worse algorithm; the risk is only in parsing.
guide.approach:
1. Full-match `name (suffix)*`; resolve the name through `refs` then as a raw id.
2. For each `(op, number)`: default number 1. For `~` step to `parents[cur][0]` that many times. For `^` with n > 0 move to `parents[cur][n-1]`.

**Dry run** `HEAD^2~1` with HEAD = M (parents E, F): `^2` moves to F; `~1` moves to F's first parent D. Result `D`. `HEAD^^^` is E, C, B.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of expression + total steps); space O(1) beyond the tokens.
guide.pitfalls: Treating `^2` as 'two generations back' (that is `~2` or `^^`). Forgetting `^0`/`~0`. Looking up raw ids before refs. Accepting junk like `HEAD~x`.
guide.follow_up: Real Git has more: `@{u}` for the upstream, `@{2}` reflog entries, `^{tree}`, `:/text` message search. On Windows `cmd`, `^` must be doubled or quoted.

git-bisect-next.title: Choose the next commit for git bisect
git-bisect-next.description:
`git bisect` hunts for the first bad commit. You tell it one **bad** commit and some **good** commits; it
repeatedly picks a commit to test that cuts the remaining suspects roughly in half.

`parents` maps commit ids to parent lists. Define the **suspects** as the commits that are ancestors of
`bad` (including `bad`) but are **not** ancestors of any commit in `good` (a good commit and all its
ancestors are cleared).

For a suspect `c`, let `x(c)` be the number of suspects that are ancestors of `c` (including `c`), and
`n` the total number of suspects. Testing `c` leaves `x(c)` suspects if it is bad and `n - x(c)` if it is good,
so its usefulness is `min(x(c), n - x(c))`.

Write `bisect_next(parents, good, bad)`:

- if there are no suspects, return `None` (contradictory input: `bad` is an ancestor of a good commit);
- if there is exactly one suspect, return it (it is the first bad commit);
- otherwise return the suspect with the **largest usefulness**, breaking ties by the smallest id.

**Example:** a line `c0 <- c1 <- ... <- c8`, `good = ["c0"]`, `bad = "c8"`: suspects are c1..c8 (n = 8) and
`x(c4) = 4`, so the answer is `"c4"`.

guide.prereqs: The lesson on debugging with bisect and blame. Ancestor sets from the earlier graph problems; binary search.
guide.intuition: On a straight line, bisect is plain binary search: test the middle. Real history is a graph, so 'the middle' needs a definition. The right question for a candidate is: if I test this commit, how many suspects survive in the worse of the two outcomes? A bad verdict keeps the candidate's own suspect ancestors; a good verdict clears them and keeps the rest. Pick the commit that balances the two.
hints: Compute the suspect set with set arithmetic: ancestors of bad minus the union of ancestors of each good commit.
For each suspect, count how many suspects lie in its ancestry (itself included).
Score each suspect by `min(x, n - x)` and take the maximum; iterate in sorted order so ties resolve to the smallest id.
guide.brute_force: The approach described is already the straightforward O(n) walks for n suspects, O(n * (V + E)) in total. Picking the middle of a sorted id list (first wrong solution) is not an algorithm for this problem at all: ids say nothing about position in history.
guide.approach:
1. `cleared` = union of ancestor sets of good commits.
2. `suspects = ancestors(bad) - cleared`.
3. For each suspect in sorted order compute `x` and the score; keep the best.

**Dry run** on the sample graph with good = [B], bad = M: suspects = {C, D, E, F, M}, n = 5. x(C) = 1, x(D) = 1, x(E) = 2 (C, E), x(F) = 2 (D, F), x(M) = 5. Scores: 1, 1, 2, 2, 0. Best score 2, smallest id `E`. If E turns out good, the suspects shrink to {D, F, M}.
guide.complexity: Time O(n * (V + E)) with n suspects; space O(V). Git computes all the counts in one pass with bitmaps for small sets and falls back to approximations on huge ranges.
guide.pitfalls: Clearing only the good commits themselves rather than their whole ancestry (second wrong solution). Returning `bad` when other suspects remain (its score is always 0). Assuming history is linear.
guide.follow_up: Each step halves the suspects, so about log2(n) tests are needed. `git bisect run <cmd>` automates the loop using the command's exit status (125 means 'skip').

git-push-check.title: Detect a non-fast-forward push
git-push-check.description:
When you push a branch, the server compares its current tip of that branch with the commit you are
sending. It accepts the update only if nothing would be lost.

`parents` is **your local** commit graph (id → parent ids). `remote_tip` is the commit the server's
branch points at now, or `None` if the branch does not exist there yet. `local_tip` is what you push.
`force` says whether you passed `--force`.

Return one of these strings from `push_check(parents, remote_tip, local_tip, force)`:

- `"new-branch"` : `remote_tip` is `None`;
- `"up-to-date"` : both tips are the same commit;
- `"fast-forward"` : `remote_tip` is an ancestor of `local_tip`;
- `"forced"` : otherwise, when `force` is true (the remote commits not in your history are discarded);
- `"rejected"` : otherwise.

Check in that order. Note that `remote_tip` may be a commit you have never fetched, in which case it does
not appear in `parents` at all and cannot be an ancestor of anything you have.

**Example:** local history `A <- B <- C`; `push_check(p, "B", "C", False)` → `"fast-forward"`.

**Example:** a teammate pushed `X` on top of B first: `push_check(p, "X", "C", False)` → `"rejected"`.
git-push-check.starter:
def push_check(parents, remote_tip, local_tip, force):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Problem *Can this branch fast-forward?* and the lesson on working with remotes.
guide.intuition: A push is a request to move a label on the server from one commit to another. Moving it forward along history loses nothing, so it is allowed. Moving it anywhere else would orphan the commits the label used to reach, so the server says no unless you insist. 'Forward along history' is exactly the ancestor test.
hints: Handle the two trivial cases (no remote branch, same commit) before any graph work.
Walk backwards from `local_tip` through all parents looking for `remote_tip`.
`force` matters only after the ancestor test has failed; a forced push that happens to be a fast-forward is still reported as a fast-forward.
guide.brute_force: Compute the complete ancestor set of `local_tip` and test membership. Same complexity class, slightly more memory than stopping at the first hit.
guide.approach:
Check `None`, check equality, then DFS from `local_tip`. Found → `fast-forward`. Not found → `forced` or `rejected` by the flag.

**Dry run**: local `A <- B <- C`, server at `X` (a teammate's commit you have not fetched). Walk from C: C, B, A, never X. Without force the push is rejected, the famous `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)`; the cure is to fetch and integrate X, then push again.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) in your local graph; space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Returning `forced` whenever the flag is set, even for clean fast-forwards. Following only first parents (the server tip may be reachable through a merge's second parent). Pushing an *older* commit over a newer one is also a non-fast-forward.
guide.follow_up: `--force-with-lease` adds one more condition: the server tip must still equal your remote-tracking ref, so you cannot wipe out work you have never seen.

git-reflog-recover.title: Recover a deleted branch from the reflog
git-reflog-recover.description:
You ran `git branch -D payments` and want the branch back. The branch's own log is gone, but the
**HEAD reflog** still records every position HEAD has had.

`entries` is the HEAD reflog **oldest first**; each entry is `[sha, message]` where `sha` is the commit HEAD
pointed at *after* the action. `start_branch` is the branch that was checked out before the first entry.

Replay the log, tracking which branch is checked out:

- A message of the form `checkout: moving from <X> to <Y>` switches the current branch to `<Y>` (take
  everything after the last `" to "`). The entry's `sha` is the tip of `<Y>` at that moment.
- Every other message (`commit: ...`, `commit (amend): ...`, `reset: moving to ...`, `merge ...`,
  `cherry-pick: ...`, ...) happens **on the current branch** and moves that branch to `sha`.

Write `recover_branch(entries, start_branch, branch)` returning the last commit that `branch` was known
to point at, or `None` if HEAD was never on that branch.

**Example:**

```
[["a1", "commit: add cart"],
 ["b7", "checkout: moving from main to payments"],
 ["c3", "commit: add stripe client"],
 ["d9", "commit: handle refunds"],
 ["a1", "checkout: moving from payments to main"]]
```

with `start_branch = "main"`: `recover_branch(e, "main", "payments")` → `"d9"`, so `git branch payments d9` restores it.

guide.prereqs: The lesson on maintenance and data recovery (reflog). Simple state machines.
guide.intuition: The reflog is a diary of HEAD. If you replay it while remembering which branch HEAD was attached to at each moment, every entry tells you where that branch pointed just then. The last such entry for the deleted branch is its final tip.
hints: Keep one variable, the current branch, and update it only on checkout entries.
Decide the order carefully: on a checkout entry the sha already belongs to the branch you moved *to*.
A commit message can contain misleading text such as `moving from a to b`; only a message that *starts* with `checkout: moving from ` is a switch.
guide.brute_force: Search the log for the last checkout *to* the branch and return that sha. This misses every commit made after switching to it, so it usually returns a stale tip.
guide.approach:
Loop over entries oldest to newest. If the message starts with the checkout prefix, set `current` to the text after the last ` to `. Then, if `current == branch`, remember `sha`.

**Dry run** on the example for `payments`: entry 1 on main; entry 2 switches to payments, last = b7; entry 3 commit, last = c3; entry 4 commit, last = d9; entry 5 switches to main. Answer d9.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) over the entries, space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Updating `last` before processing the switch (off by one entry in both directions). Parsing with `in` instead of `startswith`. Splitting on the first ` to ` rather than the last when branch names or messages contain the word.
guide.follow_up: In real life: `git reflog` to find the sha, then `git branch payments <sha>`. If the commits never touched HEAD on this machine, `git fsck --lost-found` lists dangling commits. Unreachable commits survive about 30 days by default before garbage collection may remove them.

git-lcs-diff.title: Line diff with the longest common subsequence
git-lcs-diff.description:
`git diff` shows how to turn the old version of a file into the new one with the fewest removed and added
lines. The lines that stay are a **longest common subsequence (LCS)** of the two versions.

Write `line_diff(a, b)` where `a` (old) and `b` (new) are lists of strings (lines without newlines).
Return a list of strings, each a line prefixed with two characters:

- `"  "` (two spaces) for a line kept from both versions,
- `"- "` for a line present only in `a`,
- `"+ "` for a line present only in `b`.

Several minimal diffs can exist, so use this exact rule. Let `L[i][j]` be the LCS length of `a[i:]` and
`b[j:]`. Walk with `i = j = 0`:

1. if `a[i] == b[j]`: emit a kept line and advance both;
2. else if `L[i+1][j] >= L[i][j+1]`: emit `- a[i]` and advance `i` (**deletions win ties**);
3. else emit `+ b[j]` and advance `j`.

When one list runs out, emit the remainder of `a` as deletions, then the remainder of `b` as additions.

**Example:** `line_diff(["a", "b", "c"], ["a", "x", "c"])` → `["  a", "- b", "+ x", "  c"]`

guide.prereqs: The lessons on viewing staged and unstaged changes. Two-dimensional dynamic programming (LCS).
guide.intuition: A diff is the complement of what stays the same. If you find the largest set of lines that appear in both files in the same order, everything else in the old file must be deleted and everything else in the new file must be added, and no smaller edit script exists.
hints: Fill a table `L[i][j]` = LCS length of the suffixes `a[i:]` and `b[j:]`, from the bottom-right corner upwards.
Then walk from the top-left. Equal lines are always safe to keep. Otherwise look at the two neighbouring cells to see which move keeps the LCS reachable.
The tie rule matters for the expected output: on equal values delete first. That is what makes a changed line show as `-` then `+`.
guide.brute_force: Walk both files in lock-step and call any mismatch a replace (first wrong solution). One inserted line at the top then makes every following line look changed. Enumerating all common subsequences is exponential.
guide.approach:
1. Build the suffix LCS table in O(nm).
2. Walk forward applying the three rules.
3. Flush the leftovers.

**Dry run** `a = [a, b, c]`, `b = [a, x, c]`: (0,0) equal, keep `a`. (1,1): `b` vs `x` differ; `L[2][1]` = LCS([c],[x,c]) = 1 and `L[1][2]` = LCS([b,c],[c]) = 1, tie, so delete `b`. (2,1): `c` vs `x`; `L[3][1] = 0 < L[2][2] = 1`, so add `x`. (2,2) equal, keep `c`.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(n * m) for files of n and m lines. Git's default (Myers) algorithm is O((n + m) * D) for D differences, which is much faster when files are similar.
guide.pitfalls: Building the table for prefixes and then walking forward (the directions must agree). Using `>` instead of `>=`, which flips the order of `-`/`+` pairs. Forgetting to flush the tail of both lists.
guide.follow_up: Group the output into hunks with three lines of context to get the unified format. Try `git diff --patience` or `--histogram` on moved code to see how different LCS strategies change readability.

git-apply-hunk.title: Apply a unified-diff hunk
git-apply-hunk.description:
A patch is a list of **hunks**. Each hunk starts with a header

```
@@ -<old_start>[,<old_count>] +<new_start>[,<new_count>] @@
```

followed by body lines whose first character is a space (context, present in both versions), `-`
(only in the old version) or `+` (only in the new version). A missing count means 1.

Write `apply_hunk(lines, hunk)`: `lines` is the old file as a list of strings; `hunk` is a list of strings,
header first. Return the new file as a list, or `None` if the hunk does not apply.

Rules:

- The **old side** of the hunk is its context and `-` lines in order; the **new side** is its context and `+` lines.
- The hunk is malformed (`None`) if it is empty, the header does not match the shape above, a body line starts
  with any other character (or is empty), or the header counts differ from the actual sizes of the old/new sides.
- The old side must equal `lines[old_start-1 : old_start-1+old_count]` exactly (1-based start, no fuzzy
  matching). Special case: when `old_count` is 0 the hunk only inserts, and the new lines go **after** line
  `old_start` (so `old_start = 0` inserts at the very top). The position must lie inside the file.
- `new_start` is informational; do not validate it.

**Example:**

```
lines = ["red", "green", "blue"]
hunk  = ["@@ -1,3 +1,3 @@", " red", "-green", "+lime", " blue"]
```

→ `["red", "lime", "blue"]`

guide.prereqs: Reading unified diffs (the lesson on recording changes) and the patch-based workflow in the distributed lessons.
guide.intuition: A hunk carries both versions of one region of the file interleaved: read the context plus the minus lines and you have the 'before' text; read the context plus the plus lines and you have the 'after' text. Applying it is a guarded find-and-replace: confirm the 'before' text really sits at the stated position, then splice in the 'after' text.
hints: Build two lists from the body, `old` and `new`; context lines go into both.
Slice the file at the stated position and compare it with `old` as whole lists.
A pure insertion has no old lines to anchor it, so the header's start means 'after this line' instead of 'at this line'.
guide.brute_force: Ignore the stated position and search the whole file for the old side. That is how `patch` applies hunks with an offset, but it can hit the wrong copy when a file has repeated blocks, and the task explicitly asks for exact placement.
guide.approach:
1. Parse the header with a regular expression; default counts to 1.
2. Split the body into old and new sides, rejecting unknown prefixes.
3. Check the counts.
4. Compute the zero-based position (`start - 1`, or `start` for an insertion), bounds-check, compare.
5. Return `lines[:pos] + new + lines[pos + old_n:]`.

**Dry run** of the example: header gives start 1, counts 3 and 3. Old side `[red, green, blue]`, new side `[red, lime, blue]`. Position 0; the file slice `[0:3]` equals the old side; result is the new side.
guide.complexity: Time O(len(lines) + len(hunk)) because of the list splice; space the same.
guide.pitfalls: Stripping lines (a context line may consist of spaces, and removed lines may be indented). Treating an empty body line as context. Off-by-one for insert-only hunks. Trusting the header counts without checking them.
guide.follow_up: Apply several hunks to one file: process them from the bottom up, or keep a running offset, so earlier splices do not shift later positions. `git apply --check` performs this validation for whole patches, and `git apply -3` falls back to a three-way merge.

git-three-way-merge.title: Three-way merge of line lists
git-three-way-merge.description:
Merging combines two edited versions of a file using their common ancestor. Implement a line-based
three-way merge: `merge3(base, ours, theirs)` returns `[merged_lines, conflict_count]`.

**Step 1: alignment.** Align `base` with `ours`, and `base` with `theirs`, using the longest common
subsequence found by this deterministic walk (the same rule as the *Line diff* problem): with
`L[i][j]` the LCS length of the suffixes, starting at `i = j = 0`: if the lines are equal, record the pair
`(i, j)` as matched and advance both; else if `L[i+1][j] >= L[i][j+1]` advance `i`; else advance `j`.

**Step 2: anchors.** A base line is an *anchor* if it was matched in **both** alignments. Anchors are
unchanged on both sides and cut the three files into corresponding chunks: the lines before the first
anchor, between consecutive anchors, and after the last anchor (chunks may be empty).

**Step 3: resolve each chunk** with base part `B`, our part `O`, their part `T`:

- `O == T` → output `O` (both sides agree, or neither changed);
- `O == B` → output `T` (only they changed);
- `T == B` → output `O` (only we changed);
- otherwise it is a **conflict**: output `<<<<<<< ours`, the lines of `O`, `=======`, the lines of `T`,
  `>>>>>>> theirs`, and add 1 to the conflict count.

After each chunk output the anchor line itself.

**Example:** `merge3(["a", "b", "c"], ["a", "B", "c"], ["a", "b", "c", "d"])` → `[["a", "B", "c", "d"], 0]`

**Example:** `merge3(["x"], ["ours"], ["theirs"])` →
`[["<<<<<<< ours", "ours", "=======", "theirs", ">>>>>>> theirs"], 1]`

guide.prereqs: Problem *Line diff with the longest common subsequence*; the lessons on merging and on advanced merging.
guide.intuition: The base tells you who changed what. Wherever a region is identical to the base on one side, the other side's version of that region is the intended result. Only where *both* sides differ from the base, and from each other, does a human have to decide. To find the regions, pin down the lines nobody touched (anchors); the gaps between anchors are the chunks to compare.
hints: Reuse the LCS walk, but record matched index pairs instead of printing a diff. Do it for (base, ours) and (base, theirs).
Base lines matched in both alignments are fixed points. Keep three cursors, one per file, and jump them from anchor to anchor.
Each gap gives three slices B, O, T. Four cases in a fixed order resolve it; do not forget the final gap after the last anchor.
guide.brute_force: Treat the whole file as one chunk (first wrong solution): if both sides changed anything anywhere, declare the entire file conflicted. That is how a tool without line alignment would behave and it makes merging unusable. Comparing line i with line i (second wrong solution) falls apart as soon as one side inserts a line.
guide.approach:
1. `mo`, `mt` = base-index → other-index maps from the two alignments.
2. `anchors` = sorted base indices present in both, plus a sentinel for the tail.
3. For each anchor cut `B`, `O`, `T` from the cursors up to the anchor's positions, resolve, emit, emit the anchor, move the cursors past it.

**Dry run** base `[a,b,c]`, ours `[a,B,c]`, theirs `[a,b,c,d]`: `mo = {0:0, 2:2}`, `mt = {0:0, 1:1, 2:2}`; anchors 0 and 2. Before anchor 0 all chunks empty; emit `a`. Before anchor 2: B=[b], O=[B], T=[b]; `T == B`, emit `B`; emit `c`. Tail: B=[], O=[], T=[d]; `O == B`, emit `d`. No conflicts.
guide.complexity: Time O(|base| * (|ours| + |theirs|)) for the two LCS tables; space the same.
guide.pitfalls: Checking `O == B` before `O == T` is harmless, but forgetting `O == T` reports false conflicts when both sides made the same edit. Losing the tail chunk. Counting conflict *lines* instead of conflict regions.
guide.follow_up: Add the base text between `|||||||` and `=======` to get the `diff3`/`zdiff3` conflict style, which makes conflicts far easier to resolve. `git merge-file ours base theirs` runs this algorithm on three plain files.

git-cherry-pick-conflicts.title: Predict cherry-pick conflicts from touched paths
git-cherry-pick-conflicts.description:
You want to copy some commits from a `source` branch onto a `target` branch with `git cherry-pick`. A
quick (conservative) way to predict trouble is to look only at **which files** each commit touches.

- `source`: the commits on the source branch since it forked from the target, oldest first, each
  `[commit_id, [paths it changes]]`.
- `picked`: the ids you will cherry-pick. They are always applied in **source order**, whatever order this
  list is in.
- `target_paths`: the paths changed on the target branch since the fork point.

Keep a set of **hot paths**, initially `target_paths`. Go through `source` in order:

- a commit that is **not picked** is skipped, and its paths become hot (later source commits were written
  on top of changes the target will not have);
- a commit that **is picked** conflicts on every one of its paths that is currently hot. Picking a commit
  does not change the hot set.

Return a list of `[commit_id, sorted_conflicting_paths]` for the picked commits that have at least one
conflicting path, in source order.

**Example:**

```
source = [["c1", ["api.py"]], ["c2", ["api.py", "docs.md"]], ["c3", ["ui.js"]]]
picked = ["c2", "c3"]
target_paths = ["ui.js"]
```

→ `[["c2", ["api.py"]], ["c3", ["ui.js"]]]` (c2 builds on the skipped c1; c3 collides with the target).

guide.prereqs: The cherry-pick material in the distributed-workflow and rescue lessons. Python sets.
guide.intuition: A cherry-pick replays one commit's *change* in a new place. The change applies cleanly when the surrounding file content is what the commit expects. Two things can make it differ: the target branch edited the same file, or the commit was written on top of an earlier source commit that you decided not to bring along. Both are tracked by one growing set of 'paths whose content differs from what the source expects'.
hints: Turn `picked` into a set and iterate over `source`, not over `picked`: source order is what matters.
What should happen to the hot set when you pass over a commit you are not picking?
For a picked commit, intersect its paths with the hot set and sort the result; record it only if non-empty.
guide.brute_force: For each picked commit, rescan all earlier source commits to collect skipped paths: O(n^2) set work. Maintaining one running set does it in a single pass.
guide.approach:
`hot = set(target_paths)`. For each `(id, paths)` in source order: if picked, `clash = sorted(set(paths) & hot)` and record if any; otherwise `hot |= set(paths)`.

**Dry run** of the example: hot = {ui.js}. c1 not picked → hot = {ui.js, api.py}. c2 picked, touches api.py and docs.md → clash [api.py]. c3 picked, touches ui.js → clash [ui.js].
guide.complexity: Time O(total number of paths) plus sorting the small clash lists; space O(distinct paths).
guide.pitfalls: Iterating in the order of `picked`. Forgetting skipped commits entirely (first wrong solution). Adding skipped paths only after all picks were evaluated (second wrong solution). Returning unsorted path lists.
guide.follow_up: Path overlap is a necessary but not sufficient condition: Git merges at the line level, so two edits to different parts of one file usually pick cleanly. `git cherry-pick -n` lets you try without committing, and `git range-diff` compares the picked series with the originals.

git-rebase-todo.title: Execute an interactive-rebase todo list
git-rebase-todo.description:
`git rebase -i` opens a todo list: one line per commit, oldest first, each with an action. You may reorder
lines, delete them and change the actions; Git then replays the list from top to bottom.

`commits` is the original series, oldest first, as `[id, message]` pairs. `todo` is the edited list; each
step is `[action, id]` or, for `reword`, `[action, id, new_message]`. Actions:

- `pick`: keep the commit as it is;
- `reword`: keep the commit but replace its message with `new_message`;
- `squash`: fold the commit into the **previous resulting commit**; the combined message is the previous
  message, a blank line, then this commit's message (`prev + "\n\n" + this`);
- `fixup`: fold into the previous resulting commit and **discard** this commit's message;
- `drop`: remove the commit.

A commit that does not appear in `todo` is dropped as well.

Return the resulting series, oldest first, as a list of `[ids, message]` where `ids` lists the original
commits that went into that result (in the order they were folded). Return `None` if the todo is invalid:
an unknown action, an id not in `commits`, an id used twice, or a `squash`/`fixup` with no previous
resulting commit to fold into.

**Example:**

```
commits = [["a", "add parser"], ["b", "typo"], ["c", "add tests"]]
todo    = [["pick", "a"], ["fixup", "b"], ["reword", "c", "test: cover parser"]]
```

→ `[[["a", "b"], "add parser"], [["c"], "test: cover parser"]]`

guide.prereqs: The lesson on rewriting history (interactive rebase).
guide.intuition: The todo list is a little program and you are its interpreter. Keep a result list; each instruction either appends a new result commit, modifies the last one, or does nothing. Validation is bookkeeping: known id, not seen before, known action, and something to fold into.
hints: Build a dict from id to message so lookups and the 'unknown id' check are one operation.
`squash` and `fixup` both extend the id list of `out[-1]`; they differ only in what happens to the message.
Track used ids in a set and validate *before* acting, so a bad step anywhere makes the whole result `None`.
guide.brute_force: There is no asymptotically slower sensible algorithm; the pitfalls are all in the rules. A quick hack that treats fixup like squash, or that forgets duplicate detection, passes the happy path only.
guide.approach:
Loop over steps; validate id; dispatch on the action.

**Dry run** of the example: `pick a` → `[[['a'], 'add parser']]`. `fixup b` → ids become `['a','b']`, message unchanged. `reword c` → append `[['c'], 'test: cover parser']`.
guide.complexity: Time O(len(commits) + len(todo)); space the same.
guide.pitfalls: Folding into the previous *todo line* rather than the previous *result* (they differ when the previous line was a drop). Mutating a shared list. Letting a later `drop` of an already used id pass.
guide.follow_up: Real rebase also offers `edit`, `exec`, `break`, `label`/`reset`/`merge`. `git commit --fixup=<id>` plus `git rebase -i --autosquash` writes the fixup lines for you.

git-squash-commits.title: Squash a series of commits into one
git-squash-commits.description:
A squash merge replaces a series of commits by a single commit with the same overall effect.

- `base` is the snapshot before the series: a dict `{path: content}`.
- `commits` is the series, oldest first, each `[message, changes]`, where `changes` maps a path to its new
  content, or to `None` meaning the commit deletes that path. (Deleting a path that does not exist is a no-op.)

Write `squash(base, commits)` returning `[message, changes]` for the single equivalent commit, or `None` if
`commits` is empty.

- `changes` must be **minimal**: include a path only if its final state differs from `base` (new or changed
  content → that content; present in `base` but gone at the end → `None`). A file that was added and later
  removed, or edited and then restored to its original content, must not appear.
- `message` is the first commit's message; if there are more commits, add a blank line and then one line
  `* <message>` for each of the remaining commits, joined by newlines.

**Example:**

```
base    = {"app.py": "v1"}
commits = [["add cache", {"cache.py": "c1", "app.py": "v2"}],
           ["fix cache", {"cache.py": "c2"}],
           ["revert app tweak", {"app.py": "v1"}]]
```

→ `["add cache\n\n* fix cache\n* revert app tweak", {"cache.py": "c2"}]`

guide.prereqs: Snapshots versus changes (first module) and the squash-merge discussion in *Team workflows in practice*.
guide.intuition: Git stores snapshots, not patches, and a squash is easiest to think about the same way. Do not try to 'add up' the changes. Instead play the series forward from the base to obtain the final snapshot, then compare final with base. Whatever differs is the squashed commit.
hints: Copy `base` and apply each commit's changes in order: assignment for content, removal for `None`.
The net change set is a diff of two dicts. Look at the union of their keys.
`dict.get` returns `None` for a missing key, which conveniently is also the marker for 'deleted'.
guide.brute_force: Merge all change dicts with 'later wins' (the wrong solution). It reports files that ended up identical to the base, and deletions of files that never existed before the series.
guide.approach:
1. Replay to get `final`.
2. For each path in `base` or `final`, if the contents differ record `final.get(path)`.
3. Assemble the message.

**Dry run** of the example: after the three commits `final = {app.py: v1, cache.py: c2}`. Compared with the base, `app.py` is unchanged and `cache.py` is new, so the net change is `{cache.py: c2}`.
guide.complexity: Time O(total changes + size of base); space O(size of snapshots).
guide.pitfalls: Mutating the caller's `base`. Emitting `None` for a path that was never in `base`. Forgetting that an empty series has no squash.
guide.follow_up: This is what `git merge --squash` and `git reset --soft <base> && git commit` produce. The resulting commit has a single parent, so Git no longer knows the feature branch was merged; delete the branch afterwards.

expected:
add cache

* fix cache
* revert app tweak

step 1

* step 2
* step 3
* step 4
* step 5
* step 6
* step 7

git-reset-modes.title: Simulate git reset --soft / --mixed / --hard
git-reset-modes.description:
Git keeps three "trees": the commit **HEAD** points at, the **index** (staging area) and the **working
tree**. `git reset <mode> <target>` rewinds them in stages.

Arguments of `reset(commits, head, index, worktree, mode, target)`:

- `commits`: dict `{commit_id: snapshot}` where a snapshot is `{path: content}`;
- `head`: the current commit id; `index`, `worktree`: dicts `{path: content}`;
- `mode`: `"soft"`, `"mixed"` or `"hard"`; `target`: the commit id to reset to.

Return `[new_head, new_index, new_worktree]` (do not mutate the inputs), or `None` if `target` is not in
`commits` or the mode is unknown.

- **soft**: only HEAD moves to `target`.
- **mixed**: HEAD moves and the index becomes a copy of the target snapshot. The working tree is untouched.
- **hard**: HEAD moves, the index becomes the target snapshot, and the working tree becomes the target
  snapshot **plus the untracked files**, which Git leaves alone. A working-tree path is *untracked* when it
  is neither in the **old index** nor in the **target snapshot**.

**Example:** HEAD at `c2` = `{"app.py": "v2"}`, index and working tree both `{"app.py": "v2-edited"}`,
`commits["c1"] = {"app.py": "v1"}`:

- soft to `c1` → `["c1", {"app.py": "v2-edited"}, {"app.py": "v2-edited"}]`
- hard to `c1` → `["c1", {"app.py": "v1"}, {"app.py": "v1"}]`
git-reset-modes.starter:
def reset(commits, head, index, worktree, mode, target):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Reset demystified*.
guide.intuition: Reset is three steps performed in a fixed order, and the mode says after which step to stop. Step 1 moves the branch HEAD points at. Step 2 copies that commit into the index. Step 3 copies the index into the working tree. Soft stops after 1, mixed after 2, hard does all three. The only subtlety is what 'copy into the working tree' means for files Git is not tracking.
hints: Write the soft case first, then extend: each stronger mode does everything the weaker one does plus one more overwrite.
For hard, start from a copy of the target snapshot and then decide which working-tree files survive.
A file survives a hard reset only if Git has no opinion about it: it was not staged or tracked before, and the target does not contain it.
guide.brute_force: Not applicable in a complexity sense. The naive hard reset (first wrong solution) wipes the working tree to exactly the snapshot, deleting untracked notes; the opposite mistake (second wrong solution) keeps tracked files that the target commit does not have.
guide.approach:
Validate. `soft` → copies of the old index and tree. `mixed` → target snapshot as the index. `hard` → target snapshot as both, then add every working-tree path that is in neither the old index nor the target.

**Dry run**: HEAD c3, clean, plus an untracked `notes.txt`; `hard` to c2. The snapshot of c2 is `{app.py: v2, util.py: u1}`. `docs.md` is in the old index, so it is tracked and disappears. `notes.txt` is in neither, so it stays.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(size of the snapshots).
guide.pitfalls: Returning the same dict objects that were passed in. Deciding 'untracked' with the *new* index instead of the old one. Forgetting that an untracked file with the same path as a file in the target is overwritten.
guide.follow_up: `git reset --keep` and `--merge` are safer variants that refuse to clobber local edits. `git restore` and `git switch` took over the file-level and branch-level jobs of `checkout`/`reset` in Git 2.23.

git-status-categories.title: Compute git status from three snapshots
git-status-categories.description:
`git status` is two diffs and a set difference. Given three dicts `{path: content}`:

- `head`: the snapshot of the last commit,
- `index`: the staging area,
- `worktree`: the files on disk,

write `status(head, index, worktree)` returning a dict with three sorted lists:

- `"staged"` (*Changes to be committed*, index compared with head):
  `"new file: P"` if P is in the index but not in head; `"modified: P"` if in both with different content;
  `"deleted: P"` if in head but not in the index.
- `"unstaged"` (*Changes not staged for commit*, working tree compared with the index, for paths in the index):
  `"modified: P"` if the content differs; `"deleted: P"` if P is missing from the working tree.
- `"untracked"`: the paths (just the path, no label) present in the working tree but not in the index.

Sort each list by **path**.

**Example:**

```
head     = {"a.txt": "1", "b.txt": "1"}
index    = {"a.txt": "2", "b.txt": "1", "c.txt": "new"}
worktree = {"a.txt": "3", "c.txt": "new", "tmp.log": "x"}
```

→ `{"staged": ["modified: a.txt", "new file: c.txt"], "unstaged": ["modified: a.txt", "deleted: b.txt"], "untracked": ["tmp.log"]}`

guide.prereqs: The lesson on recording changes: the three areas and the file life cycle.
guide.intuition: Status never compares the working tree with the last commit directly. It makes two adjacent comparisons: commit versus index tells you what the next commit would contain, index versus working tree tells you what you have not staged yet. A file can therefore appear in both lists at once, when you stage an edit and then edit again.
hints: Handle the three lists independently; each is a small loop.
For the staged list iterate over the union of keys of `head` and `index`.
Sort by path, not by the finished label string: `deleted: z` would sort before `modified: a`.
guide.brute_force: Comparing the working tree against HEAD (first wrong solution) merges the two stages into one and cannot express 'staged and then modified again'. It also calls a staged new file untracked.
guide.approach:
Three passes over sorted keys, exactly as the rules read.

**Dry run** of the example. Staged: `a.txt` differs (1 → 2) so modified; `b.txt` equal; `c.txt` only in index so new file. Unstaged: `a.txt` 2 vs 3 modified; `b.txt` missing on disk so deleted; `c.txt` equal. Untracked: `tmp.log`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for sorting n paths; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Sorting the label strings (second wrong solution). Calling a path untracked because it is not in HEAD. Listing a file as unstaged-deleted when it is not in the index at all.
guide.follow_up: `git status --short` prints the same information as two status letters per file; the next problem builds that format while simulating `add` and `commit`.

git-staging-sim.title: Simulate add, unstage and commit; print short status
git-staging-sim.description:
Simulate a repository that starts empty (no commits, empty index, empty working tree) and process a list
of operations:

- `["write", path, content]`: create or overwrite a file in the working tree.
- `["remove", path]`: delete the file from the working tree (no-op if absent).
- `["add", path]`: stage the working-tree state of `path`: copy its content into the index, or, if the file
  is absent from the working tree, remove the path from the index. If `path` is `"."`, do this for every
  path that is in the working tree or in the index.
- `["unstage", path]`: restore the index entry from HEAD (like `git restore --staged`): set it to HEAD's
  content, or remove it from the index if HEAD does not have the path.
- `["commit"]`: if the index differs from HEAD's snapshot, HEAD's snapshot becomes a copy of the index and
  the commit counter goes up by one; otherwise nothing happens.

Return `[commit_count, lines]` where `lines` is the final `git status --short` style report. For each path
in sorted order:

- compute `X` (index vs HEAD): `A` in the index but not HEAD, `M` in both with different content, `D` in HEAD
  but not the index, otherwise a space;
- compute `Y` (working tree vs index, only for paths in the index): `M` different content, `D` missing from
  the working tree, otherwise a space;
- if `X` or `Y` is not a space, output `X + Y + " " + path`;
- then, if the path is in the working tree but not in the index, also output `"?? " + path`.

**Example:** `[["write", "a.txt", "1"], ["add", "a.txt"], ["write", "a.txt", "2"], ["write", "b.txt", "x"]]`
→ `[0, ["AM a.txt", "?? b.txt"]]`

guide.prereqs: Problem *Compute git status from three snapshots* and the lesson on recording changes.
guide.intuition: The index is a real snapshot with its own copy of each staged file, not a list of 'files marked for commit'. `add` copies working tree → index, `commit` copies index → HEAD, `unstage` copies HEAD → index. Model the three dicts honestly and every odd-looking status (`AM`, `MM`, `D` plus `??`) falls out by itself.
hints: Keep three dicts. Each operation is one or two dict assignments or deletions.
`add` of a file that no longer exists on disk stages its *deletion*.
`commit` compares whole dicts: `index != head`. Remember to copy the index, not alias it.
guide.brute_force: Tracking only a set of 'staged file names' (the wrong solution). It commits whatever is on disk at commit time rather than what was staged, so `add`, edit, `commit` records the wrong content and the `AM`/`MM` states cannot be represented.
guide.approach:
Process operations into the three dicts, then derive the report path by path.

**Dry run** of the example: write a.txt=1; add → index {a:1}; write a.txt=2; write b.txt. HEAD is empty. For `a.txt`: in index, not in HEAD → X = `A`; working tree 2 vs index 1 → Y = `M`; line `AM a.txt`. For `b.txt`: not in index or HEAD, no XY line; in working tree and not index → `?? b.txt`.
guide.complexity: Time O(ops + paths log paths), with `add .` costing O(paths); space O(paths).
guide.pitfalls: Aliasing `head = index` so later staging silently changes history. Iterating over a dict while mutating it in `add .`. Forgetting that an edit reverted before commit makes `index == head`, so the commit is a no-op.
guide.follow_up: Real short status has more codes (`R` renamed, `C` copied, `U` unmerged, `!!` ignored). `git status --porcelain=v2` is the stable, script-friendly format.

git-stash-stack.title: Simulate the stash stack
git-stash-stack.description:
`git stash` shelves your uncommitted changes on a stack so you can switch tasks with a clean tree.

Model the uncommitted changes as a dict `dirty` `{path: content}` (empty means a clean working tree) and
the stash as a list where index 0 is the **newest** entry. Each entry has a message and a saved dict.
Process `ops` in order:

- `["edit", path, content]`: `dirty[path] = content`.
- `["push", message]`: if `dirty` is empty, record the error `"nothing to stash"`; otherwise put
  `(message, dirty)` at position 0 and make `dirty` empty.
- `["apply", n]`: if there is no entry `n`, record `"no such stash"`. If any path saved in entry `n` is
  also in `dirty`, record `"conflict"` and change nothing. Otherwise merge the saved paths into `dirty`
  (the entry stays on the stack).
- `["pop", n]`: like `apply`, and if it succeeds the entry is also removed.
- `["drop", n]`: remove entry `n`, or record `"no such stash"`.

`n` is a non-negative integer; positions shift down when an entry above is removed.

Return `[dirty, listing, errors]` where `listing` is the final stack as strings `"stash@{i}: <message>"`
(newest first) and `errors` is the list of recorded error strings in order.

**Example:** `[["edit", "a", "1"], ["push", "wip a"], ["edit", "b", "2"], ["push", "wip b"], ["pop", 1]]`
→ `[{"a": "1"}, ["stash@{0}: wip b"], []]`

guide.prereqs: The lesson on stashing and cleaning. Lists used as stacks.
guide.intuition: The stash is a stack whose top is numbered 0, so pushing renumbers everything below. Applying is a merge of saved changes into the current ones, and Git refuses when the same file is involved on both sides. Pop is 'apply, and only if that worked, drop', which is why a conflicting pop leaves the entry in place.
hints: Insert new entries at the front of a list so that list index equals stash number.
Check for a missing entry first, then for overlap, and only then change any state.
After `push`, create a *new* empty dict for `dirty`; do not `clear()` the one you just saved.
guide.brute_force: Appending to the end of the list and treating index n as position n (first wrong solution) reverses the numbering. Skipping the overlap check (second wrong solution) silently overwrites local edits, which Git never does.
guide.approach:
A loop with one branch per operation, mutating `dirty`, `stack` and `errors`.

**Dry run** of the example: edit a; push → stack [wip a], clean. edit b; push → stack [wip b, wip a], clean. `pop 1` → entry 1 is `wip a` saving {a: 1}; no overlap with the empty dirty set; dirty = {a: 1}; entry removed; stack [wip b].
guide.complexity: Time O(total paths handled) with O(k) list shifts for a stack of k entries; space proportional to the saved changes.
guide.pitfalls: Clearing the saved dict by aliasing. Dropping the entry even when the apply failed. Reporting `conflict` before `no such stash`.
guide.follow_up: Real stashes are commits: `git stash show -p stash@{0}`, `git stash branch <name>` to turn one into a branch, `git stash -u` to include untracked files, and `--index` to restore what was staged.
